questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Grandfathering and distribution
questions.learningObjective: Identify how grandfathering allocates emissions rights among existing emitters.
questions.stem: The local permit scheme gave every factory operating before 1998 a fixed free quota, a fact I noted while logging the observatory energy draw.

options.text: Existing polluters keep historic shares, so the burden follows past output rather than present need.
Free quotas mean nobody has to pay for the pollution each factory creates.
options.misconception: thinks grandfathered permits remove the cost of emitting

options.text: Grandfathering cancels the cap, so total emissions return to their historical level.
options.misconception: assumes grandfathering cancels the binding cap

options.text: The scheme is progressive, because early factories had to wait longer for their permits.
options.misconception: believes early permits imply a progressive outcome

questions.explanation: Grandfathering decides who holds emission rights, not how many are issued. It can lock in historic pollution patterns and create windfall rents. Older factories did not wait longer for permits.
questions.hint: Focus on who holds the rights, not the cap level.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Price ceilings and over-emission
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a price ceiling produces emissions above the allowance cap.
questions.stem: I charted how the regional allowance price was capped at 12 dollars a tonne, after which firms demanded 150 million tonnes of allowances.

options.text: The price cap guarantees firms never exceed the emissions cap, since prices and quantities are linked.
options.misconception: confuses a price cap with a binding quantity limit

options.text: Because the price is capped, every allowance issued must find a buyer.
options.misconception: assumes a fixed price guarantees full demand

options.text: Firms emitted 150 million tonnes against 100 million issued allowances, since the capped price made extra emissions cheap.
Over-emission here reflects a shortage of fuel rather than any policy effect.
options.misconception: blames fuel scarcity instead of the price ceiling

questions.explanation: A binding price ceiling lowers the cost of emitting below the level needed to meet the cap, so firms over-emit. Here 150 Mt emitted against 100 Mt issued is exactly that 50 Mt gap.
questions.hint: Ask what the controlled price does to abatement.

questions.topic: Testing a feebate with a holdout
questions.learningObjective: Compute a difference in differences from a feebate pilot and a holdout.
questions.stem: The log records a feebate pilot: treated drivers averaged 12.2 litres per 100 km before and 10.4 after, while a random holdout went from 12.0 to 11.2.
questions.explanation: The difference in differences is (10.4 - 12.2) minus (11.2 - 12.0), giving -1.8 minus -0.8, that is -1.0 litres per 100 km. The holdout absorbs weather and fuel price shocks.
questions.hint: Compare the change, not the levels.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Checking a reported emissions cut
questions.learningObjective: Assess what a reported emissions reduction actually demonstrates.

stimulus.body: Our team reports that the facility emissions fell 10 percent in 2025 against the 2023 baseline. Fifty thousand tonnes of the reduction came from buying certified offsets. A reviewer asked whether the operational changes would have happened anyway.

questions.stem: The letter in my notebook claims the facility cut emissions by 10 percent, so I need to judge what that reported figure establishes.

options.text: The claim is verified, because the baseline year and current year were measured by the same team.
options.misconception: treats matching measurement teams as proof

options.text: The claim is verified, since 10 percent is the threshold the plant licence requires.
options.misconception: confuses a regulatory threshold with verification

options.text: The claim is rejected outright, because any use of offsets invalidates a reduction claim.
options.misconception: assumes all offset use disqualifies a claim

options.text: Part of the drop is purchased offsets, so the direct cut is 10000 of 500000 tonnes, or 2 percent.

questions.explanation: The 10 percent headline includes 50000 offset tonnes, leaving an operational cut of 10000 out of 500000 tonnes, or 2 percent. Verification must also test additionality and permanence.
questions.hint: Strip out purchased offsets before judging the cut.

questions.topic: A fuel standard applied to a plant record
questions.learningObjective: Design a fair comparison of emissions between production shifts.
questions.stem: A plant record lists fuel use for two shift patterns, and I want a fair comparison of emissions intensity before writing it into my log.

options.text: Compare emissions per tonne of product for each shift over several weeks, using metered fuel and measured output.
Compare total monthly emissions for each shift, because absolute tonnes are what the public cares about.
options.misconception: prefers absolute totals that ignore output

options.text: Compare fuel use per shift against the manufacturer brochure figure for the same engine.
options.misconception: relies on brochure data instead of metered use

options.text: Compare one shift in winter against one shift in summer, avoiding the need for separate baselines.
options.misconception: confuses seasonal variation with shift performance

questions.explanation: Per-unit intensity removes shift size from the comparison, and metered fuel avoids default-factor error. Totals confound output with efficiency, and brochure data misses real consumption.
questions.hint: Normalise by something the shift actually produced.

questions.topic: Delivering a stated finance commitment
questions.learningObjective: Judge whether a stated finance pledge has actually been delivered.
questions.stem: A climate fund told my club it had pledged 500 million dollars over five years, and I asked how much had been paid out.

options.text: The full 500 million counts as delivered, since pledges become binding once announced.
options.misconception: treats announced pledges as money disbursed

options.text: Delivery is complete, because the fund reports the same pledged figure each year.
options.misconception: confuses a repeated figure with verified delivery

options.text: Nothing can be judged yet, because disbursement data appears only after the fund closes.
options.misconception: believes disbursement data waits until closure

options.text: Only 185 million was disbursed, so the delivery rate against the pledge is 37 percent.

questions.explanation: A pledge is a promise and a disbursement is cash paid, so 185 of 500 million is 37 percent delivered. Repeating the pledge figure proves nothing, and interim disbursement data is usually published.
questions.hint: Separate promises from cash actually paid.

questions.topic: Additionality in an offset project
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the additional reduction of an offset project against its baseline.
questions.stem: The offset file lists business-as-usual emissions of 240000 tonnes for the year, actual emissions of 200000 with the project running, and a claimed credit of 60000 tonnes.
questions.explanation: The additional reduction is baseline minus actual, so 240000 minus 200000 is 40000 tonnes, and only that is claimable. Claiming the full 60000 tonnes credits a cut that would have happened anyway.
questions.hint: Additionality compares actual with the no-project case.

questions.topic: Revenue recycling in a carbon tax
questions.learningObjective: Select a revenue recycling arrangement that is fair and durable.
questions.stem: The observatory log records a local carbon tax of 25 dollars per tonne on fuel sales, with 2 million tonnes of fuel sold in the year.

options.text: Spend the whole 50 million on new bus lanes, so nothing is returned to the households paying the tax.
options.misconception: assumes only spending schemes recycle revenue fairly

options.text: Return the 50 million collected as per-household rebates, keeping the price signal and sharing the burden.
Keep the revenue in a reserve fund, because rebates would blunt the incentive to cut emissions.
options.misconception: believes rebates blunt the incentive to reduce

options.text: Cut the tax rate to zero and fund the transition from general taxation instead.
options.misconception: thinks abandoning the tax avoids the fairness problem

questions.explanation: Revenue is 25 dollars times 2 million tonnes, or 50 million dollars. Targeted rebates offset costs for exposed households while the price signal still works, and fairness buys durable support.
questions.hint: Recycling must offset who pays the tax.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Design of a self-determined target regime
questions.learningObjective: Identify the design features that make self-set targets credible.
questions.stem: At the regional meeting I jotted notes on a self-determined target regime where each signatory sets its own reduction target.

options.text: Targets are credible as long as each signatory is legally obliged to submit one each cycle.
options.misconception: believes submitting a target guarantees ambition

options.text: Targets are credible if they follow the most ambitious signatory, so effort is uniform.
options.misconception: confuses common ambition with comparable rules

options.text: Targets are only credible if they are transparent, comparable across signatories, and ratcheted up over time.
Targets are credible once a pledge is signed, because pledges cannot be revised after ratification.
options.misconception: assumes signed pledges can never be revised

questions.explanation: Self-determined targets work only if rules enforce disclosure, comparable accounting, review, and a ratchet. A duty to submit says nothing about ambition, and good regimes expect revisions.
questions.hint: What stops weak targets hiding behind strong ones?

questions.learningObjective: Compare a sector performance standard with an economy-wide price.
questions.stem: The paper I am reading sets a uniform carbon price for the economy but a separate intensity standard for the cement sector.

options.text: The uniform price is always better, because one price removes the need to design any sector rule.
options.misconception: assumes a single price is always preferable

options.text: The standard is better because it delivers a lower carbon price for that sector.
options.misconception: confuses an intensity standard with a price exemption

options.text: The standard is better because it removes the need to measure the sector's actual emissions.
options.misconception: believes standards remove the need for measurement

options.text: The standard fixes emissions intensity per tonne of clinker, giving a known path while the price covers the rest.

questions.explanation: An intensity standard fixes a measurable limit as output changes, giving firms a clear target. A uniform price instead gives cost certainty and lets each firm choose its own abatement.
questions.hint: Ask what each instrument guarantees to the firm.

questions.topic: Grandfathering and distribution
questions.learningObjective: Convert historic emission shares into shares of a cap.
questions.stem: Under our grandfathering scheme the cap is 120 million tonnes and historic shares are 50, 30 and 20 percent for the three plants.

options.text: Each plant may emit its historic output, so the total rises to 150 million tonnes.
options.misconception: thinks grandfathering grants fixed tonnage

options.text: The largest plant holds 60 million tonnes, exactly its historic 50 percent share of the 120 million cap.
The plants split the cap in equal thirds, so each receives 40 million tonnes.
options.misconception: assumes grandfathering equalises historic shares

options.text: The cap only binds when total historic output exceeds 120 million tonnes.
options.misconception: confuses a cap with a trigger on historic output

questions.explanation: Grandfathering converts historic shares into shares of the cap, so half of 120 million tonnes is 60 million tonnes. It grants no fixed tonnage, does not equalise the plants, and the cap still binds.
questions.hint: A share of the cap is not a fixed tonnage.

questions.topic: Price ceilings and over-emission
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a binding price ceiling loosens an allowance cap.
questions.stem: The log entry for the trading scheme notes an allowance price cap of 10 dollars a tonne against an expected market price of 30.

options.text: The price cap guarantees exactly the promised reduction, since prices and quantities are fixed together.
options.misconception: believes a price cap pins down emissions

options.text: The price cap holds emissions at the level implied by the 30 dollar market price, so nothing changes.
options.misconception: assumes a price cap does not change behaviour

options.text: The price cap simply removes the need for a fixed number of allowances, because prices replace the cap.
options.misconception: thinks a price cap replaces a quantity cap

options.text: At the capped price firms over-emit, because abatement now costs more than the capped 10 dollars a tonne.

questions.explanation: A binding price cap pushes allowance prices below the level where firms would abate, so they emit more than the cap allows. Fixing price does not fix quantity, and dropping the cap changes the scheme.
questions.hint: Think about what a low price does to abatement.

questions.topic: Testing a feebate with a holdout
questions.learningObjective: Explain the role of a randomised holdout in a feebate trial.
questions.stem: In my log I describe a feebate pilot where a random tenth of eligible drivers are held out from the fee for a year.

options.text: The held-out tenth gives the counterfactual, so the change in their behaviour estimates what the feebate avoided.
The held-out tenth increases total emissions of the pilot, because those drivers now face no charge.
options.misconception: thinks a holdout adds avoidable emissions

options.text: The held-out tenth proves the feebate works only if those drivers are later charged the same fee.
options.misconception: believes fairness requires recharging the holdout

options.text: The held-out tenth is unnecessary, since the pilot can compare mean fuel use before and after.
options.misconception: dismisses the control group as redundant

questions.explanation: A randomised holdout supplies the counterfactual of what would have happened without the fee, so comparing changes measures the effect. Before-and-after comparisons lack a control.
questions.hint: The holdout stands in for the policy's absence.

questions.topic: A fuel standard applied to a plant record
questions.learningObjective: Apply a standard fuel factor to a plant consumption record.

stimulus.body: The plant log for March shows 45000 litres of diesel consumed by the kiln line. The standard factor on file is 2.68 kg of carbon dioxide per litre of diesel, taken from a national default set. Actual production that month was 1800 tonnes of clinker.

questions.stem: Using the memo, what emissions should I record for the kiln line, and what should I check first?

options.text: 120.6 tonnes, from 45000 litres at 2.68 kg each, and I must check the factor is for diesel.
120.6 tonnes is right, and no check is needed because national default factors never need review.
options.misconception: assumes default factors are always applicable

options.text: 48.2 tonnes, because the factor must be applied to production rather than to fuel consumed.
options.misconception: divides emissions by output instead of using fuel

options.text: The figure should be left blank until metered fuel data replace the monthly record.
options.misconception: treats an incomplete record as a reason to skip

questions.explanation: 45000 litres times 2.68 kg per litre is 120600 kg, or 120.6 tonnes, and the factor must describe diesel. A default factor stands in for a known fuel, not a reason to leave the record blank.
questions.hint: Fuel times factor, then check the fuel matches.

options.misconception: treats repeated announcements as delivery evidence

options.misconception: assumes project counts track disbursed funds

options.text: Compare administrative spending with project spending, since lean administration signals strong delivery.
options.misconception: treats low overhead as proof of delivery

options.text: Publish the recycling formula, run a distributional analysis first, and recycle a fixed share to households each year.

options.text: Recycle the money through a general fund cut, so no new spending commitments need to be made.
options.misconception: treats a spending cut as equivalent recycling

questions.topic: Delivering a stated finance commitment
questions.learningObjective: Calculate programme funds available after overhead.
questions.stem: A fund's table shows 250 million dollars committed, 175 million disbursed, and a 10 percent administration charge on disbursed funds.

options.text: About 175 million reaches programmes, because administration is funded elsewhere, not from the fund.
options.misconception: assumes overhead never comes from the fund

options.text: About 250 million reaches programmes, because committed money is available whenever projects need it.
options.misconception: treats committed money as immediately spendable

options.text: About 157.5 million reaches programmes, once a 10 percent administration charge is taken off the 175 million paid.
About 225 million reaches programmes, because only the gap between committed and disbursed is overhead.
options.misconception: infers overhead from the commitment gap

questions.explanation: A 10 percent charge on 175 million disbursed removes 17.5 million, leaving 157.5 million for programmes. Committed money is not cash and the gap between committed and disbursed is not the overhead figure.
questions.hint: Apply the overhead rate to money actually paid out.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Additionality in an offset project
questions.learningObjective: Identify the no-project behaviour that reduces creditable volumes.
questions.stem: I am reviewing a cookstove project's claim that it avoided a large volume of fuelwood use compared with open fires.

options.text: Ask how many stoves were sold, because the credited volume follows the number of units delivered.
options.misconception: links credited volume to units sold

options.text: Ask the price paid for the credits, because buyers only pay for genuine additional reductions.
options.misconception: assumes buyers verify additionality for you

options.text: Ask how confident the project staff are, since they know the community best.
options.misconception: relies on project staff confidence

options.text: Ask how many households would have switched anyway, because that switch reduces the credited volume.

questions.explanation: Additionality is measured against the no-project switch rate, so the share moving to cleaner stoves must be known before volumes are credited. Units sold and staff confidence describe the project, not the baseline.
questions.hint: Find the no-project switch rate for the area.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Revenue recycling in a carbon tax
questions.learningObjective: Calculate a household rebate from carbon tax revenue and recycling.
questions.stem: A carbon charge of 22 dollars a tonne on 3600000 tonnes of fuel sales raises revenue, and 80 percent is returned equally to 158400 households.
questions.explanation: Revenue is 22 times 3600000, or 79200000 dollars, and 80 percent is 63360000 dollars. Over 158400 households the rebate is 400 dollars each, far below the revenue raised.
questions.hint: Recycled revenue divided by households gives the rebate.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Design of a self-determined target regime
questions.learningObjective: Specify the discipline a self-set target regime needs.
questions.stem: In my reading of the regime's rules, signatories set their own targets but must report progress every two years.

options.text: The rules should require independent verification of every target before it is accepted into the record.
options.misconception: assumes every target needs external verification

options.text: The rules should also require comparable accounting, review and a ratchet, so self-set targets stay ambitious.
The rules should set a single common target for all signatories, replacing self-determination entirely.
options.misconception: proposes replacing self-determination with one target

options.text: The rules should drop the reporting requirement, since reporting costs fall hardest on poorer signatories.
options.misconception: assumes reporting costs justify removing scrutiny

questions.explanation: Self-set targets need comparability, review and a ratchet, so weak ambition cannot hide behind strong ambition. Verifying every target is too heavy, and dropping reporting removes the checks entirely.
questions.hint: Self-declared targets need external discipline.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Standard against uniform price for one sector
questions.learningObjective: Compare a uniform carbon price with a sector performance standard.
questions.stem: Write a short comparison, for the observatory newsletter, of an economy-wide carbon price against a performance standard for one sector.

answer.exemplar: A uniform carbon price gives cost certainty, lets each firm find its cheapest abatement and needs little sector-specific data. A performance standard gives a known emissions intensity path and rewards early movers, but it needs reliable measurement and careful setting to avoid locking in the current split of output.

questions.explanation: A strong comparison names what each instrument guarantees, cost certainty against intensity certainty, and the data and distribution questions that follow. Simply preferring one instrument misses the comparison.
questions.hint: Compare what each instrument guarantees.
